en.title: Estate Management: the whole course
en.short: What estate management covers, how degree courses are organised, and how to study property well.

sections.heading: What estate management is
sections.text:
Estate management is the study and practice of land and buildings as property. It covers how rights in land are held, how property is valued, managed, developed, financed, marketed, taxed and regulated. It draws on economics, law, planning, construction, accounting and data. It is wider than selling houses: a manager may run leases, a valuer may advise a bank, and a development surveyor may test a site’s viability.

The work is local. Property law, planning rules, taxes and professional registration differ by country. In Nigeria, estate surveying and valuation are regulated by the Estate Surveyors and Valuers Registration Board of Nigeria (ESVARBON), and the profession is represented by the Nigerian Institution of Estate Surveyors and Valuers (NIESV). Other countries use other titles and bodies. Always check the current national regulator.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length and awards differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, a BSc Estate Management is commonly a five-year full-time degree, though entry route and industrial training arrangements vary. Polytechnics may offer National Diploma (ND) and Higher National Diploma (HND) routes. After the degree, professional registration usually requires further practical experience and assessment; check ESVARBON and NIESV for current requirements.

In the UK, a BSc Real Estate or Estate Management is commonly three years full-time, with some sandwich courses lasting four; many are accredited by the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS). A master’s, often one year full-time in the UK, can convert other graduates. Read your handbook and regulator’s website, because names, durations and rules change.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics give tools and context. Mathematics and quantitative methods support valuation and investment calculations. Economics for property explains markets, rent and land use. Legal foundations cover property law, and building construction technology explains how buildings are made and measured. Surveying and mapping deal with site and location data. Urban and regional planning introduces land use and development. Management and accounting principles cover property firms, and property data and information technology covers records, maps and software.

Core topics then apply these tools. Land tenure and property rights explain who owns what. Valuation principles and methods teach the main approaches to value. Property market analysis and urban land economics explain prices, rents and location. Real estate finance and investment cover loans, yields and risk. Advanced valuation covers investment, development and specialist property. The development process links site finding, appraisal, construction and sale. Construction cost and procurement deal with contracts and cost control. Property management and lease administration, facilities management and maintenance cover running buildings. Planning law and development control, property taxation and rating, and compulsory acquisition and compensation cover public rules and payments. Housing policy and delivery, real estate agency and marketing, and professional practice and ethics complete the core.

Master’s topics add advanced valuation theory and uncertainty, investment and portfolio management, sustainable real estate and climate risk, and research methods for a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the vocabulary, then use it in calculations and short cases. For valuation, write the formula, list the inputs, show units and check whether the answer is sensible. For law and planning, link each rule to the country and to a practical situation such as a lease, a development application or a compulsory acquisition.

Practise with real documents where possible: a lease, a title document, a valuation report, a planning notice. Keep a glossary of terms and a file of worked examples. Use spreadsheets for cash flows, but be able to reproduce the arithmetic by hand. Read property news with care, and ask which market and year the figures refer to. Site visits and industrial training are part of the course.

en.title: Introduction to Estate Management
en.short: Land, property and real estate, stakeholders, careers, professional bodies and the property life cycle.

sections.heading: Core terms
sections.text: Estate management is the profession that advises on and manages land and buildings: buying, selling, letting, valuing, developing, maintaining and using them. Real estate means land and the permanent structures on it, such as houses, shops and offices. Land is the surface, the soil below and the space above, with the rights attached. Property is wider: anything owned, though in property work it usually means rights and interests in land and buildings. A lease is property; a chair is not real estate.

sections.heading: Scope and roles
sections.text: The scope includes valuation, agency, property management, facilities management, development, investment advice and research. Owners hold title and decide use; occupiers live or trade in the property, often under a lease; investors buy for income or capital gain; government plans, regulates, taxes and may acquire land for public purposes. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state in the governor, who holds it in trust for the common benefit of all Nigerians. In the United Kingdom, most land is freehold or leasehold. Rules differ, so check the country.

sections.heading: Careers and bodies
sections.text: Career paths include estate surveyor or valuer, property manager, facilities manager, real estate agent, development manager, investment analyst and researcher. Professional bodies and registration differ by country. Nigeria has the Nigerian Institution of Estate Surveyors and Valuers (NIESV) and the Estate Surveyors and Valuers Registration Board of Nigeria (ESVARBON). The United Kingdom has the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS). Confirm current requirements with the official body.

sections.heading: Life cycle case
sections.text: The property life cycle runs from land acquisition and feasibility through design, construction, letting, occupation, management and repair to refurbishment, redevelopment or demolition. Case: Amina owns a shop in Kano. She leases it to a trader, the occupier. A local investor buys the building from Amina for rental income. The government controls planning permission and taxes property. The investor may hire an estate manager to collect rent and arrange repairs. Each stage needs different skills.

keyPoints: Estate management covers the valuation, management, development, sale and letting of land and buildings.
Real estate is land and permanent structures; property is broader and includes rights and interests.
Owners hold title, occupiers use the property, investors seek income or gain, and government regulates and taxes.
The property life cycle runs from acquisition and feasibility to construction, occupation, management and eventual redevelopment.
Professional bodies and registration differ by country; in Nigeria they include NIESV and ESVARBON, and in the UK the RICS.
Check current registration and legal requirements with the official body in the country concerned.

en.title: Mathematics and Quantitative Methods for Estate Management
en.short: Arithmetic, measurement, interest, present value and statistics for property data.

sections.heading: Numbers and measurement
sections.text: Arithmetic covers adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing. Algebra uses letters for unknown values and lets you rearrange formulas. A ratio compares two quantities, such as a plot 25 m by 40 m, written 25:40 or 5:8. A percentage is a fraction of 100: 5:8 is 62.5%. Indices are powers, so 10² = 10 × 10 = 100. A graph plots one variable against another; the slope shows change per unit. In property work, keep units consistent before calculating.

sections.heading: Area and volume
sections.text: Area is the size of a surface; volume is the space inside a solid. For a rectangle, area = length × breadth. A plot 25 m × 40 m has area 1,000 m². For a cuboid, volume = length × breadth × height. A store 10 m × 8 m × 3 m has volume 240 m³. Triangles, circles and irregular shapes need their own formulas or surveying methods. Always state the unit: m² for area, m³ for volume.

sections.heading: Interest and present value
sections.text: Simple interest is I = P × r × n, where P is principal, r the annual rate as a decimal and n years. On ₦500,000 at 10% for 2 years: I = 500,000 × 0.10 × 2 = ₦100,000, total ₦600,000. Compound interest adds interest to principal each year: FV = P(1 + r)ⁿ. Here FV = 500,000 × 1.10² = ₦605,000. Present value reverses this: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ. So ₦605,000 due in 2 years at 10% is worth 605,000 ÷ 1.21 = ₦500,000 today.

sections.heading: Property data
sections.text: Basic statistics summarise data. The mean is the total divided by the count. The median is the middle value when ordered. The range is highest minus lowest. Example rents in ₦000: 200, 250, 300, 350, 400. Mean = 1,500 ÷ 5 = 300; median = 300; range = 400 − 200 = 200. Graphs and tables help compare rents, yields and floor areas, but check units, dates and missing values before drawing conclusions.

keyPoints: Keep units consistent; area uses m² and volume uses m³.
Rectangle area = length × breadth; cuboid volume = length × breadth × height.
Simple interest: I = P × r × n; compound future value: FV = P(1 + r)ⁿ.
Present value: PV = FV ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ.
Mean = total ÷ count; median = middle ordered value; range = highest − lowest.
Check data units, dates and missing values before interpreting property figures.

en.title: Economics for Property
en.short: Demand, supply, elasticity, cost, market structure and macro policy applied to property.

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.text:
Demand is the quantity buyers will take at each price; supply is the quantity sellers offer. In property, demand is derived from need for housing, shops and offices, and land supply is relatively fixed in the short run.

A local rent is an equilibrium price. Above it, vacant units pull rent down; below it, queues and bidding push rent up. Location, transport and planning rules shift demand or restrict supply.

sections.heading: Elasticity and cost
sections.text:
Price elasticity of demand measures responsiveness: PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price. Example: annual rent rises from ₦200,000 to ₦220,000 and demand falls from 100 to 95 units. %ΔQ = −5%, %ΔP = 10%, so PED = −0.5. Demand is inelastic, so landlords’ revenue rises.

Income elasticity compares demand with income. Costs include fixed and variable costs, marginal cost and opportunity cost, the value of the next best use of land or capital.

sections.heading: Market structure
sections.text:
Market structure ranges from perfect competition, many small sellers with identical goods, to monopoly, one seller, oligopoly, few sellers, and monopolistic competition, many sellers with different products.

Property markets are local, heterogeneous and information is imperfect, so they sit far from perfect competition. Estate managers compare rents, yields and costs within these structures.

sections.heading: Macro and policy
sections.text:
Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level; it erodes the real value of fixed rents. Interest rates affect mortgage payments and the rate used to discount future income. National income, measured by gross domestic product (GDP), influences demand for space.

Government policy works through fiscal tools such as taxes and spending, and monetary tools such as the policy rate. The Central Bank of Nigeria sets the monetary policy rate; the Bank of England in the UK sets Bank Rate. Higher rates usually weaken property prices, but timing and country conditions vary; check current official sources.

keyPoints: Demand and supply set local rents; land supply is relatively fixed in the short run.
PED = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in price; demand is inelastic if the value lies between −1 and 0.
Income elasticity = % change in quantity demanded ÷ % change in income.
Costs include fixed, variable, marginal and opportunity cost.
Market structures range from perfect competition to monopoly; property markets are local and imperfect.
Inflation, interest rates, national income and government fiscal and monetary policy all affect property demand, rents and values; current rates and rules differ by country.

en.title: Legal Foundations of Property
en.short: Sources of law, courts, real and personal property, tenure, easements, covenants, mortgages and registration.

sections.heading: Sources and courts
sections.text: Law comes from legislation, case law, custom and, in some countries, religious law. Nigeria’s sources include the Constitution, statutes such as the Land Use Act 1978, court decisions, customary law and, in some northern states, Islamic law. Courts apply these sources. Legal reasoning means reading a statute, following precedent (earlier decisions), and separating the ratio decidendi (the reason for a decision) from obiter dicta (comments not binding). Land law differs by country, so check the local statutes and courts.

sections.heading: Property and rights
sections.text: Real property means land and things fixed to it, such as buildings. Personal property means movable things, such as cars. Ownership is the legal right to use and dispose of property. Possession is physical control, which may exist without ownership, as with a tenant. Tenure is the system under which land is held. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state governor, who holds it in trust, and people hold rights of occupancy. This is not universal; England and Wales use freehold and leasehold estates.

sections.heading: Dealings and registration
sections.text: An easement is a right over another person’s land, such as a right of way. The land benefited is the dominant tenement; the land burdened is the servient tenement. A covenant is a promise in a deed about land, often restricting use. A mortgage secures a loan on property; if the borrower fails to pay, the lender may enforce it. Registration records title or transactions in a public register. Some countries register deeds; others register title, as under the Torrens system. Registration supports certainty but does not cure every defect.

sections.heading: Short example
sections.text: In Nigeria, Ada buys a registered plot and grants Bello a right of way across it. Ada holds a right of occupancy over the plot; Bello has an easement. If Ada mortgages the plot to a bank and fails to repay, the bank may enforce the mortgage. If Ada promised not to build a shop, that covenant may bind later owners if registered. The result depends on Nigerian law and the register.

keyPoints: Land law differs by country; check local statutes and court decisions.
Sources of law include legislation, case law and custom, and courts apply precedent and statutory interpretation.
Real property is land and fixtures; personal property is movable.
Ownership is the legal right to property; possession is physical control.
Tenure is the system by which land is held; an easement is a right over another’s land.
A covenant is a promise about land; a mortgage secures a loan; registration records title or dealings.

en.title: Building Construction Technology
en.short: Materials, substructure, superstructure, services and defects, and how construction affects cost, value and maintenance.

sections.heading: Materials and structure
sections.text:
Building materials include blocks, concrete, steel, timber, glass and roofing sheets. Their strength, durability and maintenance needs differ. The substructure is the part below ground, mainly the foundation and ground slab. It carries loads and resists settlement and damp. The superstructure is above ground: columns, beams, walls, floors and roof. Floors may be concrete slabs or timber; walls may be load-bearing or non-load-bearing; roofs may be pitched or flat. A damp-proof course stops rising moisture.

In Nigeria, the National Building Code and state planning rules are references, but status and enforcement vary; check the current official version. Professional registration, such as COREN for engineers in Nigeria, also differs by country.

sections.heading: Services and defects
sections.text:
Building services include water supply, drainage, electricity, ventilation and fire safety. Poor services cause damp, leaks and unsafe buildings. Common defects are cracks from settlement, dampness from failed waterproofing or drainage, roof leaks, termite attack in timber, and spalling concrete, which means the surface breaks away, often where the steel inside has rusted. Some defects are structural and need an engineer. Regular inspection and maintenance protect value.

A made-up case: a durable roof costs NGN 2,000,000 more but saves NGN 250,000 a year in repairs. Payback = 2,000,000 ÷ 250,000 = 8 years. This ignores inflation and the time value of money.

sections.heading: Cost, value and management
sections.text:
Construction choices affect cost, value, maintenance and management. A cheap building may cost less now but more later. Good foundations, drainage and roofs reduce repair bills and keep tenants. Quality materials and services raise initial cost but can raise rent and resale value.

Estate managers need drawings, approvals and maintenance records. They should check that work meets the approved plans and local code before accepting it. Defects found late can become expensive disputes.

keyPoints: Substructure is below ground and carries loads; superstructure is above ground.
Materials and workmanship affect strength, durability and maintenance cost.
Building services must be designed and installed safely.
Common defects include damp, cracks, leaks and termite damage.
National building codes and professional registration differ by country; check the current official source.
Extra durable construction can be justified by payback = extra cost ÷ annual saving.

en.title: Surveying and Mapping for Property
en.short: Measuring land, levelling, traverses, GNSS, maps, coordinates, area and site plans for property.

sections.heading: Measuring on site
sections.text: Linear measurement is the direct or indirect measurement of distance, using a tape or an electronic distance meter (EDM). Levelling finds height differences with a level and staff; it may use the height of instrument or rise and fall method. If a backsight on a benchmark reads 1.250 m and a foresight reads 1.750 m, the second point is 1.750 − 1.250 = 0.500 m lower. Traversing measures connected lines and angles from known points; a closed traverse returns to its start, and any misclosure is adjusted before coordinates are accepted.

sections.heading: Maps, coordinates and area
sections.text: GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) fixes positions from satellites; survey-grade receivers with differential correction or RTK (real-time kinematic) can reach centimetre level, while handheld units are less precise. Map reading uses scale, grid, north arrow and contours. Scale is the ratio of plan distance to ground distance: 60 mm at 1:500 represents 60 × 500 = 30,000 mm = 30 m. Coordinates are eastings and northings. Area from coordinates uses Area = ½ |Σ(x_i y_{i+1} − x_{i+1} y_i)|. For A(0,0), B(30,0), C(30,20), D(0,20), the sum is 0 + 600 + 600 + 0 = 1,200, so area = 600 m².

sections.heading: Site plans and title
sections.text: A site plan is a scaled drawing showing boundaries, buildings, access and services. Survey plans support title registration by defining the parcel; development by fixing boundaries, levels and drainage; and valuation by proving area and frontage. A cadastral system records parcels for ownership and taxation, and such systems differ: England and Wales use registered title at HM Land Registry; Australia uses Torrens title; Nigeria uses state land registries and survey plans checked by the state Surveyor-General, with requirements varying by state. Always check the local survey and registration rules.

keyPoints: Linear measurement gives distances; levelling gives height differences; traversing fixes points by connected lines and angles.
A closed traverse must be adjusted for misclosure before coordinates are accepted.
GNSS with differential correction or RTK can give survey-grade positions; handheld units are less precise.
Scale: ground distance = plan distance × scale denominator.
Area from coordinates: Area = ½ |Σ(x_i y_{i+1} − x_{i+1} y_i)|.
Survey plans define parcels for title, guide development, and support valuation; cadastral rules differ by country.

en.title: Introduction to Urban and Regional Planning
en.short: Settlement patterns, land use, zoning, planning process and how planning shapes property supply and value.

sections.heading: Settlements and land use
sections.text: Urban and regional planning guides land use and development across a city or region. A settlement pattern is how buildings and people are spread out: nucleated (clustered), dispersed, linear along roads, or grid layouts. Land use is the activity allowed on a parcel: housing, shops, offices, industry, schools, open space or mixed use. In many African cities, planned areas sit beside informal settlements built without formal approval. Planning coordinates roads and services and separates incompatible uses, such as a factory beside homes.

sections.heading: Zoning and control
sections.text: Zoning is a public rule that divides land into zones and states permitted uses, density (units per hectare), height and setbacks. It shapes property supply: housing land cannot normally become a shopping centre. It also shapes value: commercial zoning on a busy road may raise land value, while conservation rules may limit redevelopment. The planning process usually runs through survey, plan preparation, public participation, adoption, implementation and review. Development control checks each proposal against the plan. A developer seeks planning permission; the authority may approve, refuse or attach conditions, and enforcement stops unauthorised building. Names and laws differ by country, so check the local planning authority.

sections.heading: Supply, value and use
sections.text: Planning affects supply by releasing land, setting density and requiring infrastructure. A made-up case: a council zones 20 hectares for low-density housing at 10 dwellings per hectare. The plan allows 20 × 10 = 200 dwellings. If demand is high and little land is released, plot prices may rise. If the same land were zoned for apartments at higher density, more units could be supplied, which may ease prices. Planning can also cut value by restricting use or reserving land for roads and parks. Abuja, Lagos, Nairobi and Accra show planned expansion beside informal growth.

keyPoints: Urban and regional planning coordinates land use, infrastructure and services across space.
Settlement patterns include nucleated, dispersed, linear and grid layouts.
Land use is the activity on a parcel; zoning sets permitted uses, density, height and setbacks.
The planning process runs from survey and plan preparation through adoption, implementation and review.
Development control checks proposals against the plan through permissions, conditions and enforcement.
Dwellings allowed = site area in hectares × permitted density in dwellings per hectare; planning restrictions can raise or lower property value.

en.title: Management and Accounting Principles for Property Firms
en.short: Management functions, business forms, budgets, financial statements and ratios for property firms.

sections.heading: Management and structure
sections.text: Management is planning, organising, leading and controlling resources to meet goals. A property firm plans its workload, organises staff and files, leads through the principal or manager, and controls by comparing results with plans. Business forms include sole proprietorship, partnership and limited liability company. The right form depends on liability, capital and tax rules, which differ by country. In Nigeria, estate surveying firms are regulated by ESVARBON, and the professional body is NIESV; rules differ elsewhere. A small firm may use a functional structure: valuation, property management, accounts and administration. Larger firms may group by office or client, or use a matrix for projects.

sections.heading: Budgets and statements
sections.text: A budget is a money plan. An operating budget covers income and expenses; a cash budget shows expected receipts and payments; a capital budget covers long-term purchases. Variance is actual minus budget. Financial statements report performance and position. The income statement shows revenue less expenses for a period. The statement of financial position lists assets, liabilities and equity at a date. The cash flow statement explains cash movements. For a property firm, revenue includes management fees, valuation fees and commissions. Expenses include salaries, office rent and transport. Client money, such as rents collected for owners, must be kept in a separate client account, not mixed with the firm’s own money.

sections.heading: Ratios and client money
sections.text: Ratio analysis turns figures into tests of performance. Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. A result above 1 suggests short-term bills can be met. Net profit margin = net profit ÷ revenue. Debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ equity; it shows how much a firm relies on borrowing. Example: a firm has current assets ₦8,000,000, current liabilities ₦4,000,000, revenue ₦20,000,000 and net profit ₦3,000,000. Current ratio = 8,000,000 ÷ 4,000,000 = 2.0. Net profit margin = 3,000,000 ÷ 20,000,000 = 0.15, or 15%. Client accounts need separate records, regular bank reconciliation and segregation of duties, so the person who records receipts is not the same person who banks them. Professional office practice also requires confidentiality and safe keeping of files.

keyPoints: Management functions are planning, organising, leading and controlling.
Business forms include sole proprietorship, partnership and limited liability company, and rules differ by country.
A budget is a money plan; variance is actual minus budget.
The income statement shows profit, the statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity, and the cash flow statement shows cash movements.
Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities; net profit margin = net profit ÷ revenue; debt-to-equity = total debt ÷ equity.
Client money must be held in a separate client account with proper records and segregation of duties.

en.title: Property Data and Information Technology
en.short: Spreadsheets, databases, CAD, GIS and online property data, with data quality, security and ethics.

sections.heading: Core digital tools
sections.text: Four tools do most of the digital work. A spreadsheet holds rows and columns and recalculates formulas when data changes. A database stores many linked records and answers queries, such as all leases ending this year. Computer-aided design (CAD) draws and edits plans, sections and site layouts. A geographic information system (GIS) links data to maps so you can compare locations, distances and boundaries. Online property data includes portals, government registers and market reports; their coverage and reliability differ by country, so check the source.

sections.heading: Supporting property work
sections.text:
These tools support daily estate work. A spreadsheet rent roll lists units, tenants, rents and vacancies and totals them. A database keeps maintenance histories and lease dates and can flag renewals. Valuers use databases and online data to find comparable sales and record adjustments. GIS helps market analysis by showing price patterns near roads, schools or flood zones. CAD drawings help with space planning and reporting. Online data speeds up comparable searches, but you must record the date and source.

Case: a manager in Enugu tracks 12 flats. Ten are let at ₦120,000 a month and two are vacant. Monthly rent = 10 × 120,000 = ₦1,200,000. Annual rent = 1,200,000 × 12 = ₦14,400,000. If yearly expenses are ₦3,600,000, net income = 14,400,000 − 3,600,000 = ₦10,800,000. A spreadsheet updates these figures at once.

sections.heading: Quality, security and ethics
sections.text: Good data is accurate, complete, consistent and current. Errors in a rent figure or a boundary can mislead a client. Security means limiting access, using strong passwords, backing up files and protecting personal data. Data protection laws differ by country; for example, Nigeria has the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, but you should check the current rules where you work. Ethics covers confidentiality, consent, honest reporting and declaring the source of online data. Do not copy a listing or a map without permission.

keyPoints: Spreadsheets calculate and update figures; databases store linked records and answer queries.
CAD draws plans; GIS links data to maps for location analysis.
Online property data varies by country and must be checked for date and source.
Good data is accurate, complete, consistent and current.
Security includes access control, backups and protection of personal data.
Ethics requires confidentiality, consent and honest reporting.

en.title: Land Tenure and Property Rights
en.short: Customary, statutory, freehold, leasehold and public tenure, title registration, encumbrances and compulsory acquisition.

sections.heading: Tenure types
sections.text:
Tenure is the set of rules for holding rights in land. Customary tenure is held under customary law, by a family or community, with group ownership and individual use rights. Statutory tenure is created by legislation, such as a right of occupancy in Nigeria. Freehold is an estate of indefinite duration; leasehold is a fixed term, usually with rent and a reversion. Public tenure is land held by government for public purposes.

In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in each state in the governor, who grants statutory rights of occupancy; local governments grant customary rights. Most new interests are now rights of occupancy rather than freehold. Tenure law differs by country.

sections.heading: Title and registration
sections.text:
Title is evidence of a right to land; it is not tenure. Registration records title in a public register. In Nigeria, state land registries record titles, and a Certificate of Occupancy is evidence of a statutory right of occupancy. Not all customary land is registered. In England and Wales, HM Land Registry records freehold and leasehold titles. Ghana’s Land Act 2020 recognises customary and statutory interests and provides for registration through the Lands Commission.

An encumbrance is a right or burden that limits the owner, such as a mortgage, lease, easement, covenant or caveat. A buyer checks for encumbrances because they can survive a sale. Registration practice differs by country.

sections.heading: Acquisition and case
sections.text:
The state may compulsorily acquire land for a public purpose, subject to compensation. The power and procedure are set by national or state law; in Nigeria, the Land Use Act and state laws apply.

Case: a family in Aba, Nigeria, holds farmland under customary tenure. A developer wants to buy it. The lawyer checks whether the family’s interest is recorded, whether the land is under a right of occupancy, and whether any mortgage or caveat encumbers it. The deal may fail if the family cannot show a registered title, even though customary rights are recognised.

keyPoints: Tenure is the rules by which rights in land are held; customary, statutory, freehold, leasehold and public tenure are common types.
In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 vests land in state governors, who grant statutory rights of occupancy, while local governments grant customary rights.
Title is evidence of a right; registration records title, and a Certificate of Occupancy evidences a Nigerian statutory right of occupancy.
Encumbrances such as mortgages, leases, easements, covenants and caveats can bind later buyers, so they must be checked.
Compulsory acquisition is a state power for public purpose, subject to compensation, and its procedure is set by national or state law.
Tenure law and registration practice differ by country; do not apply Nigerian rules elsewhere.

en.title: Valuation: Principles and Methods
en.short: Purpose and bases, market, cost, income and profits approaches, process, evidence and report structure.

sections.heading: Purpose and bases
sections.text: A valuation is an opinion of value at a stated date. The purpose, such as sale, mortgage, compensation or financial reporting, decides the basis. Market value is the estimated amount for an exchange between a willing buyer and seller in an arm’s length transaction after proper marketing, each acting knowledgeably, prudently and without compulsion. Other bases include market rent, investment value and fair value. The International Valuation Standards (IVS), published by the International Valuation Standards Council, give a common framework. National standards and mandatory bases differ by country: the RICS Red Book is issued by RICS, a UK-based body, and applies to its members worldwide; USPAP applies in the US; and in Nigeria check current ESVARBON and NIESV requirements.

sections.heading: Approaches
sections.text: The market or comparison approach adjusts prices of similar sold properties for differences in location, size, condition and date. The cost approach adds land value to replacement or reproduction cost and deducts depreciation; it suits special buildings with few sales. The income approach capitalises net operating income (income after operating expenses but before finance and tax), or discounts future cash flows, and suits let property. The profits approach values the trading potential of a business property, such as a hotel or filling station, separating tangible assets from goodwill. Choose the method that fits the property, evidence and purpose.

sections.heading: Process and report
sections.text: Agree instructions and terms of engagement: client, purpose, basis, property, date and fees. Inspect, measure, collect comparable evidence and analyse market conditions. Keep a file of sources. A report normally states the property, purpose and basis, valuation date, inspection details, method, evidence, assumptions, limitations, opinion of value and valuer’s signature. It must be clear enough for another valuer to follow.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A shop produces net operating income of NGN 1,200,000 a year. The market capitalisation rate is 8%. Value = income ÷ rate = 1,200,000 ÷ 0.08 = NGN 15,000,000. Check: 15,000,000 × 0.08 = 1,200,000.

keyPoints: Purpose and basis must be agreed before valuation; standards and mandatory bases differ by country.
The market approach adjusts comparable sale prices for differences.
Cost approach: value = land value + depreciated replacement cost.
Income approach: value = net operating income ÷ capitalisation rate.
The profits approach values trading potential, separating tangible assets from goodwill.
A report states property, purpose, basis, date, method, evidence, assumptions and value.

en.title: Property Market Analysis
en.short: Segments, demand and supply, rents, yields, vacancy, cycles and indicators for property markets.

sections.heading: Segments and data
sections.text:
Property markets are analysed in segments because residential, commercial, industrial and agricultural property have different users and data. Residential demand depends on households, income and credit; commercial on business activity and employment; industrial on trade, logistics and infrastructure; agricultural on commodity prices, rainfall, tenure and credit. Supply responds through new construction, conversion and demolition, usually with a lag.

Use official statistics, land registries, valuation and agency records, listings and professional surveys. In Nigeria, the National Bureau of Statistics and state land registries are starting points; in England and Wales, HM Land Registry publishes transaction data and the Valuation Office Agency publishes rental statistics. Check definitions and coverage before comparing places.

sections.heading: Rents and vacancy
sections.text:
Market rent is the rent a property would let for in the open market; passing rent is the rent actually paid under a lease. Demand and supply set both rent and vacancy. Vacancy rate = vacant space ÷ total space × 100, counted by floor area or by units. A small office block has 20 units and 2 are vacant: 2 ÷ 20 × 100 = 10%. High vacancy weakens landlords’ bargaining power; low vacancy supports rent growth.

Indicators include take-up (space let or sold in a period), absorption (net change in occupied space), construction pipeline and transaction volume. Compare them with rents and incentives such as rent-free periods.

sections.heading: Yields and cycles
sections.text:
Yield = annual net rent ÷ capital value × 100, where net rent is rent after operating costs but before finance and tax. If annual net rent is ₦12,000,000 and value is ₦150,000,000, yield = 12,000,000 ÷ 150,000,000 × 100 = 8%. For a given rent, yields move inversely with capital values. Property cycles are often described as recovery, expansion, oversupply and recession; timing and depth vary by country and segment.

For simple analysis, track rents, yields, vacancy, take-up and supply over several years, adjust for inflation, and compare like with like. A single year can mislead.

keyPoints: Vacancy rate = vacant space ÷ total space × 100, by floor area or by units.
Yield = annual net rent ÷ capital value × 100.
Market rent is set by demand and supply; passing rent is the lease rent.
Property cycles are often described as recovery, expansion, oversupply and recession, but timing varies.
Residential, commercial, industrial and agricultural segments have different demand drivers.
Use official data and like-for-like comparisons; check definitions and coverage.

en.title: Urban Land Economics
en.short: Location theory, bid rent, land use competition, agglomeration and urban growth.

sections.heading: Location and bid rent
sections.text:
Land value depends on location because location gives access. Location theory says firms and households choose sites that balance rent against travel and other costs. Bid rent is the most a user can pay for a site and still make a normal profit. It falls with distance when transport costs rise. A retailer bids more near customers; a manufacturer may prefer a peripheral site with good roads.

Example: a shop earns 120,000 per month after all costs except rent and transport. Transport costs 10,000 per km. At 2 km, bid rent = 120,000 − (2 × 10,000) = 100,000. At 5 km, it is 120,000 − (5 × 10,000) = 70,000. The bid rent curve slopes down.

sections.heading: Land use competition
sections.text: Different uses compete for the same land. The use that can bid the highest rent wins, often called highest and best use. This explains why city centres have high-density commercial buildings and why housing spreads outward. Density responds to land price: developers build upward where land is expensive, if construction and planning costs allow. In many African cities, formal and informal land markets operate side by side, and infrastructure such as roads and water shapes which sites can be developed.

sections.heading: Agglomeration and growth
sections.text: Agglomeration economies are savings that firms gain by locating near one another: shared suppliers, labour pools and knowledge. They raise productivity and bids for land, pulling activity into clusters. But congestion and high rents push some activities out. Urban growth follows investment in transport and utilities, population growth and migration. In African cities, rapid growth often outpaces infrastructure, so accessibility varies sharply between well-served and poorly served areas.

keyPoints: Bid rent is the maximum rent a user can pay and still make a normal profit.
Bid rent = income after all costs except rent − (transport cost per km × distance).
Land tends to go to the use with the highest bid rent, called highest and best use.
Density rises where land values are high, if construction and planning costs allow.
Agglomeration economies lower costs and raise land values in clusters.
Accessibility and infrastructure drive urban land values and growth, especially in fast-growing African cities.

en.title: Real Estate Finance and Investment
en.short: Time value, cash flows, NPV, IRR, mortgages, leverage and risk in property investment.

sections.heading: Cash flows and discounting
sections.text: A property investment is a stream of cash flows: purchase cost, rents, expenses and sale proceeds. Money has a time value: cash today can earn a return, so cash later is worth less. Discount each flow to present value: PV = CF ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ, where r is the discount rate and n the year. Net cash flow is income minus outgoings. Use after-tax cash flows and state the timing.

sections.heading: NPV and IRR
sections.text: NPV adds present values of cash flows; initial cost is negative at year 0. Accept if NPV is positive at the required return. The internal rate of return (IRR) is the discount rate that makes NPV zero; accept if IRR exceeds the hurdle rate. IRR can mislead if cash flows change sign more than once. Example: a property costs 10,000,000, gives net rents of 1,200,000 at the end of each of three years, and sells for 9,500,000 at the end of year 3. At 10%: PV = 1,200,000 ÷ 1.1 + 1,200,000 ÷ 1.1² + (1,200,000 + 9,500,000) ÷ 1.1³ = 10,121,713. NPV = 10,121,713 − 10,000,000 = +121,713.

sections.heading: Mortgages and leverage
sections.text: A mortgage is a loan secured on property; rules differ by country, so check current terms. Leverage means using borrowed money. It raises return on equity when the property’s income return exceeds the mortgage rate, but magnifies losses. Example: a 20,000,000 property is bought with 5,000,000 equity and a 15,000,000 interest-only mortgage at 12%. Net operating income is 2,500,000. Interest = 15,000,000 × 0.12 = 1,800,000. Cash flow to equity = 2,500,000 − 1,800,000 = 700,000. Return on equity = 700,000 ÷ 5,000,000 = 14%. Unlevered yield = 2,500,000 ÷ 20,000,000 = 12.5%.

sections.heading: Risk and comparison
sections.text: Risk is the chance that actual cash flows differ from expectation. Property risks include vacancy, arrears, repairs, illiquidity and interest-rate changes. Real estate is illiquid and costly to trade, but it can produce income and diversify a portfolio of shares and bonds. Compare investments on NPV, return, risk and liquidity, not yield alone.

keyPoints: PV = CF ÷ (1 + r)ⁿ discounts a future cash flow.
NPV = Σ PV of cash flows − initial cost; accept positive NPV at the required return.
IRR is the discount rate where NPV = 0; compare it with the hurdle rate.
Leverage raises return on equity when income return exceeds mortgage rate, but magnifies losses.
Mortgage interest = loan × rate; cash flow to equity = net operating income − debt service.
Real estate is illiquid and risky; compare it with other assets on NPV, return, risk and liquidity.

en.title: Advanced Valuation: Investment, Development and Specialist Property
en.short: Investment and residual methods, leasehold and freehold values, development appraisal and uncertainty.

sections.heading: Investment method
sections.text:
The investment method capitalises a property’s net income into capital value: value = net income ÷ yield. It suits property bought for its rent. The yield, or capitalisation rate, is drawn from comparable sales and reflects risk and expected growth. For a fixed term, years’ purchase YP = (1 − (1+i)⁻ⁿ) ÷ i.

Example: net income ₦2,400,000 at an 8% yield gives 2,400,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₦30,000,000.

sections.heading: Residual method
sections.text:
The residual method values a site by deducting all development costs and profit from the completed value, called the gross development value (GDV). It suits land with development potential where no comparable site exists. Developer’s profit is often a percentage of GDV or of total development costs.

Example: GDV ₦120,000,000; construction ₦70,000,000; fees ₦8,000,000; finance and contingency ₦6,000,000; profit 20% of GDV = ₦24,000,000. Residual land value = 120 − 70 − 8 − 6 − 24 = ₦12,000,000, before purchase costs.

sections.heading: Leasehold and freehold
sections.text:
A freehold interest lasts indefinitely, so its income is capitalised in perpetuity: value = income ÷ yield. A leasehold interest ends, so only the profit rent (rent received less ground rent paid) is capitalised over the remaining term; the reversion belongs to the freeholder. Leaseholds are therefore worth less than freeholds.

Example: 10 years remain, rent ₦1,000,000, ground rent ₦200,000, yield 10%. Profit rent ₦800,000 × YP(10 years, 10%) = 800,000 × 6.1446 ≈ ₦4,915,700.

sections.heading: Specialist property
sections.text: Specialist property such as hotels, petrol stations and plant rarely sells, so market evidence is thin. Valuers use the profits method, capitalising a fair maintainable operating profit, or depreciated replacement cost (replacement cost less an allowance for age and wear) for owner-occupied assets. Because inputs are estimates, good practice gives a range, tests sensitivity and states assumptions. Professional standards, such as the RICS Red Book used in the UK and many other countries, and guidance from the Nigerian Institution of Estate Surveyors and Valuers, set requirements; check the current edition for your country.

keyPoints: Investment method: value = net income ÷ yield, with the yield taken from comparable sales.
Years’ purchase for a term: YP = (1 − (1+i)⁻ⁿ) ÷ i.
Residual method: land value = GDV − construction − fees − finance − developer’s profit.
A leasehold is valued on its profit rent for the remaining term, so it is worth less than the freehold.
Use the residual method for development sites, and the profits or replacement cost methods where market evidence is thin.
Report uncertainty as a range, state assumptions, and follow the current professional standard in your country.

en.title: Property Development Process
en.short: From site search and appraisal to consent, finance, construction and sale.

sections.heading: Stages and team
sections.text: Property development is the process of improving land or buildings to create value. It runs from site identification and a feasibility study, through acquisition, planning consent, finance, construction and marketing, to disposal or retention. A feasibility study tests whether a scheme is practical and profitable. The development team usually includes the developer, estate surveyor, architect, engineer, quantity surveyor, planner, lawyer, financier and contractor. The developer coordinates them and carries the main risk; roles and procurement routes differ by country.

sections.heading: Appraisal and risk
sections.text: Project appraisal estimates value, cost, time and profit before money is committed. The residual method is common: site value = gross development value (GDV) minus construction and professional costs minus developer’s profit. Example: GDV ₦120,000,000; costs ₦70,000,000; profit set at 20% of GDV = ₦24,000,000; residual site value = ₦26,000,000. This is before acquisition costs, finance and taxes. Risks include planning refusal, cost overrun, delay, interest-rate change and weak demand. Developers use contingencies, phased finance, pre-lets and options to manage them.

sections.heading: Consent and finance
sections.text: Planning consent is country-specific. In Nigeria, applications go to state or local planning authorities under state planning law; in England and Wales, to the local planning authority under the Town and Country Planning Act 1990. Conditions may be attached, and refusal can be appealed. Finance also follows national rules. Sources include bank loans, equity partners, retained profits and, in some countries, listed property vehicles such as REITs. Lenders usually require appraisals, consent, cost plans and pre-sales. In Nigeria, securities and collective investment schemes are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission; check current rules.

sections.heading: Construction to disposal
sections.text: After consent and finance, construction is procured and supervised. Marketing may start before completion. Disposal can mean sale, lease or retention for income. A post-completion review compares outturn with appraisal. The process is cyclical: new information can send the developer back to earlier stages.

keyPoints: Development runs from site identification and feasibility through acquisition, consent, finance, construction and marketing to disposal or retention.
The development team is led by the developer and includes surveyors, architects, engineers, planners, lawyers, financiers and contractors.
Residual appraisal: site value = GDV − construction and professional costs − developer’s profit.
Planning consent and development finance rules are country-specific, so check the current official source.
Risk is managed with contingencies, phased finance, pre-lets and options.

en.title: Construction Cost and Procurement
en.short: Cost estimating, cost planning, bills of quantities, tendering, procurement and development viability.

sections.heading: Estimating and planning
sections.text:
Cost estimating predicts construction cost from drawings, specifications and measured quantities. Approximate quantities measure key elements and multiply by current rates. Cost planning controls cost from inception through design by setting budgets, preparing elemental cost plans and comparing tenders with the budget. Include contingency for unknown ground, design changes and price changes, plus professional fees where appropriate.

Example: 1,200 m² at 500 currency units/m² = 600,000. Add 10% contingency: 600,000 × 1.10 = 660,000. Add 8% fees: 660,000 × 0.08 = 52,800. Total = 712,800. Rates and fees vary by country and year.

sections.heading: Bills and tendering
sections.text:
A bill of quantities (BoQ) itemises work, describes each item and measures its quantity from drawings and specifications. Tenderers price each item. A priced BoQ helps compare bids, value interim payments, price variations and settle final accounts. It does not guarantee final cost, because quantities and work can change. In design and build, a specification and schedule of rates may replace it.

Tendering invites priced offers. Open tendering advertises publicly; selective tendering invites a shortlist; negotiated tendering discusses price with chosen contractors.

sections.heading: Procurement and viability
sections.text:
Procurement is the wider choice of how design, construction and risk are organised. Traditional design-bid-build separates design from construction. Design and build gives one contractor responsibility for both. Management contracting and construction management use specialist managers. Each route allocates risk differently and affects price certainty, speed and disputes.

Construction cost affects viability. Using the example, cost 712,800 plus land 50,000 = 762,800. If completed value is 780,000, surplus is 17,200 before finance. A 5% tender premium of 35,640 makes cost 748,440 plus land 50,000 = 798,440, above value. Standard contracts such as FIDIC, JCT, NEC and AIA allocate risk, but editions and law differ by country.

keyPoints: Cost estimating predicts cost; cost planning controls it against a budget.
Estimate = measured quantity × rate, plus contingency and fees.
A bill of quantities is a measured, itemised schedule that tenderers price.
Tendering methods include open, selective and negotiated.
Procurement route affects risk allocation, price certainty, speed and disputes.
Surplus = completed value − total development cost; a small cost rise can remove viability.

en.title: Property Management and Lease Administration
en.short: Landlord and tenant duties, leases, rent review, service charges, arrears, records and client reporting.

sections.heading: Lease and licence
sections.text: A lease gives a tenant exclusive possession for a fixed term, usually for rent. A licence only gives permission to use the property and creates no estate. The lease sets out the parties, term, rent, review pattern, service charge, repair duties and permitted use. Read it with local landlord and tenant law, which differs by country. In Nigeria, most rules are state-based, and Lagos State has a Tenancy Law 2011; England uses statutes such as the Housing Act 1988. Check the current law.

sections.heading: Duties and rent
sections.text: The landlord must give quiet enjoyment (the right to use the property without disturbance), maintain common parts and structure where the lease says so, insure if required, and account for money received. The tenant must pay rent, repair the interior, comply with covenants and seek consent before assignment or subletting. Rent review adjusts rent at stated intervals. It may be fixed, index-linked or to open market value, and may be upward only. Residential tenancies often have statutory protection; commercial leases are commonly longer and may be full repairing and insuring (FRI). Public property may be held under allocation or licence with public accountability.

sections.heading: Service charges and arrears
sections.text: A service charge is the tenant’s share of costs for common parts and services. The lease or statute sets the apportionment, often by floor area. Example: total annual service charge is 1,200,000 and total floor area is 2,000 m². A flat of 100 m² pays 100 ÷ 2,000 = 5%, so 5% × 1,200,000 = 60,000. Arrears are rent or charges unpaid when due. Age them monthly, send reminders, and follow the lease and law before forfeiture (ending the lease for breach) or court action.

sections.heading: Records and reporting
sections.text: Good management keeps a rent roll, tenancy schedule, service charge budget and accounts, arrears ageing, maintenance log and correspondence. These records support decisions and show the client that money is controlled. Report regularly to the landlord or client on occupancy, income, arrears, expenditure, repairs and risks. Keep personal and commercial data confidential. In public property, add transparency and procurement records.

keyPoints: A lease grants exclusive possession for a term; a licence does not.
Landlord and tenant duties come from the lease and from country-specific law, so check the current statute.
Rent review may be fixed, index-linked or open market, and may be upward only.
Service charge share = tenant floor area ÷ total floor area × total service charge.
Arrears are unpaid rent or charges; age them and follow the lease and law before enforcement.
Keep a rent roll, tenancy schedule, service charge accounts and arrears report, and report regularly to the client.

en.title: Facilities Management and Maintenance
en.short: Planned and reactive maintenance, building services, safety, space and lifecycle cost.

sections.heading: Maintenance and value
sections.text:
Facilities management (FM) coordinates the buildings, services and support that let an organisation use space safely and productively. It protects asset value by keeping fabric and systems working, and supports occupiers through cleaning, security, comfort and reliable services.

Maintenance is planned or reactive. Planned maintenance is scheduled before failure: preventive work such as servicing, and condition-based work triggered by inspection or sensor data. Reactive maintenance repairs breakdowns. Planned work usually costs less over time and causes fewer disruptions, though reactive cover is still needed.

sections.heading: Services and safety
sections.text:
Building services are the mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) systems: heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC), lighting, lifts, water, drainage, fire detection and suppression, security and information and communication technology (ICT). Good maintenance keeps them reliable, energy-efficient and compliant.

Health and safety duties are country-specific. In Nigeria, the Factories Act sets workplace duties; in the UK, the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 does so. FM teams use risk assessments, permits to work and safe systems of work. Engineering work may require registration, for example with the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN). Check current local law and registration rules.

sections.heading: Space and lifecycle cost
sections.text:
Space management allocates and uses space: measuring occupancy (people present) and utilisation (how intensively space is used), planning moves, and sometimes charging departments for the area they use. Good space data reduce waste and support hybrid or flexible working.

Lifecycle cost, or whole life cost, adds capital, operating, maintenance, replacement and disposal costs, preferably discounted to present value:
LCC = capital + Σ(operating + maintenance) + replacement − residual value.

Example: Pump A costs ₦2,000,000 installed and ₦550,000 a year to run and maintain. Pump B costs ₦2,500,000 and ₦330,000 a year. Over 10 years, ignoring discounting:
A = 2,000,000 + 10 × 550,000 = ₦7,500,000
B = 2,500,000 + 10 × 330,000 = ₦5,800,000
B is cheaper by ₦1,700,000 despite its higher purchase price.

keyPoints: FM coordinates building services, space and support to protect asset value and help occupiers work safely.
Planned maintenance is scheduled before failure; reactive maintenance repairs breakdowns and usually costs more.
Building services include MEP, HVAC, lifts, water, fire systems and ICT; maintenance affects reliability, energy and compliance.
Health and safety and engineering registration are country-specific; check current local law and rules such as COREN in Nigeria.
Space management uses occupancy and utilisation data to allocate space and reduce waste.
Lifecycle cost = capital + Σ(operating + maintenance) + replacement − residual value; discount future costs to present value.

en.title: Planning Law and Development Control
en.short: Planning legislation, development plans, permits, zoning, enforcement and appeals, with Nigeria as the main example.

sections.heading: Law and plans
sections.text: Planning law is the set of statutes, regulations and local rules governing land use and building. It differs between countries, and even within a country. In Nigeria, the main federal statute is the Nigerian Urban and Regional Planning Act 1992, but court decisions have made planning largely a state matter, so each state has its own planning law and local governments share some control. The 1992 Act applies mainly in the Federal Capital Territory and to federal projects, and provides for planning authorities and development plans. A development plan is a public document that maps proposed land uses, roads, densities and services for an area over a period. It guides decisions but does not itself grant permission.

sections.heading: Permits and zoning
sections.text: Development control is the day-to-day process of checking proposed building and land-use changes against the plan and the law. A developer usually needs a development permit, often called planning permission or building plan approval, from the relevant planning authority, which may be a state or local government body. The application includes site plans, drawings and evidence of title. Zoning divides land into use zones, such as residential, commercial, industrial and open space, and sets limits on height, coverage and setbacks. A permit may be refused or granted with conditions.

sections.heading: Enforcement and appeals
sections.text: Enforcement begins when work starts without a permit or breaks its conditions. The authority may issue a contravention or stop-work notice, then require correction, and in serious cases the building may be demolished. Appeals let an applicant challenge a refusal, a condition or an enforcement notice. In Nigeria, appeal routes are set by state law and may go to a planning tribunal or the state government; check the current law because procedures differ.

sections.heading: Case example
sections.text: Consider a made-up case in Lagos. Amina applies to build a two-storey shop on land zoned residential. The authority refuses because the zone allows only low-density housing and the plan reserves the site for a school. She appeals under state law, and the appeal body allows a small ground-floor shop with conditions on parking and drainage. If she later builds a third floor without approval, the authority can serve an enforcement notice.

keyPoints: Planning law and procedures differ between countries and often within one country.
A development plan guides land use but does not itself grant permission.
A development permit is the formal approval needed before most building or change of use.
Zoning separates land uses and sets limits such as height, coverage and setbacks.
Enforcement notices can stop unauthorised work and may lead to correction or demolition.
Appeal routes are set by national or state law, so check the current law.

en.title: Property Taxation and Rating
en.short: Land and property taxes, rating, assessment, exemptions and who bears the burden.

sections.heading: Taxes and rating
sections.text: Property tax is a recurring tax on the ownership or occupation of land and buildings; transfers of property may attract separate one-off taxes. A land tax falls on land value alone; a property tax may include buildings. Rating is a local property tax charged on the assessed value of a property, usually paid by the occupier or owner. The rules are country-specific: in Nigeria, local government councils levy tenement rates under state laws, while England uses council tax on dwellings and business rates on non-domestic property. Rates and reliefs change, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Assessment and exemptions
sections.text: Assessment is the process of fixing the tax base, often called rateable value. It may use annual rental value, capital value or floor area. A revaluation updates values to a common date. Exemptions and reliefs reduce the base: common examples are places of worship, charities, public buildings and sometimes agricultural land, but each country defines its own. Example: rateable value = 4,000,000; rate = 1.25% (1.25 per 100 of value). Annual tax = 4,000,000 × 0.0125 = 50,000. If the rate were 2%, tax = 80,000.

sections.heading: Incidence and effects
sections.text: Tax incidence is who really bears the cost, which may differ from the legal payer. A tax on land tends to be capitalised into lower land prices; a tax on buildings may raise rents or reduce development. Higher holding taxes discourage land banking but can also deter investment if poorly administered. For local government, property rates are a stable own-source revenue, but collection is often weak. Good valuation rolls, clear exemptions and fair appeals support both revenue and accountability. The tax base and rate must be published and appeals handled independently.

keyPoints: Property tax is a recurring tax on land and buildings; rating is its local form, based on assessed value.
Assessment fixes the rateable value, using rental value, capital value or floor area, and revaluation keeps it current.
Annual tax = rateable value × rate, for example 4,000,000 × 0.0125 = 50,000.
Exemptions and reliefs vary by country and reduce the tax base; check the current law.
Tax incidence may fall on owners through lower capital values or on occupiers through higher rents.
Property rates can support local government finance, but need fair valuation, clear rules and good collection.

en.title: Compulsory Acquisition and Compensation
en.short: Public acquisition, public purpose, due process, compensation valuation and resettlement, with Nigeria as an example.

sections.heading: Public purpose
sections.text: Compulsory acquisition is the state’s power to take private interests in land, with or without the owner’s consent, for a public purpose. Public purpose means a use that serves the public, such as a road, school or hospital. Some countries also allow taking for private projects that serve a public benefit. The exact list differs by country. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 gives state governors power to revoke a right of occupancy for overriding public interest. A right of occupancy is a legal right to use and occupy land.

sections.heading: Due process
sections.text: Due process means following the legal steps before land is taken. The authority must have legal power, identify the land and interest taken, give the required notice, allow objections where the law provides, value the loss, and pay compensation as the statute requires. Taking possession before payment may be unlawful in some countries; the rule varies. A public aim alone is not enough. If the procedure is defective, an owner may challenge the acquisition in court. Compensation rules differ by country, so check the current law and official guidance.

sections.heading: Compensation and resettlement
sections.text: Compensation is payment for the interest taken and the loss caused. Valuation for compensation assesses each compensable head. Common heads include market value of the land or lease, replacement cost of buildings and unexhausted improvements, value of crops, and disturbance, which covers losses from being forced to move. Unexhausted improvements are works on the land that still have value, such as a well, fence or building. In Nigeria, the Land Use Act provides compensation for buildings and unexhausted improvements at replacement cost, for crops, and for the rent paid on the land. Resettlement is the process of moving people and restoring their housing, land and livelihoods. It raises issues of alternative land, timing, transport, income and vulnerable groups. Cash may not replace farmland if no land is available. Made-up example: crops valued at ₦450,000 plus unexhausted improvements valued at ₦1,200,000 give compensation of ₦450,000 + ₦1,200,000 = ₦1,650,000. A resettlement package may add land or housing, but the rules differ by country.

keyPoints: Compulsory acquisition is the state’s taking of private interests in land for a public purpose under legal power.
Public purpose must serve the public; some countries also allow taking for private projects with a public benefit, and the exact list differs by country.
Due process requires legal authority, notice, a chance to object where the law allows, valuation and payment under the statute.
In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 lets state governors revoke a right of occupancy for overriding public interest and provides compensation for buildings, unexhausted improvements and crops.
Compensation rules and heads differ by country, so check the current law and official guidance.
Total compensation is the sum of the valued compensable items; resettlement may also be needed to restore housing and livelihoods.

en.title: Housing Policy and Delivery
en.short: Housing demand, tenure, affordability, social housing, self-build and delivery policy tools.

sections.heading: Demand and tenure
sections.text:
Housing demand is the number of homes households want at a given price and income; need is what they require for decent shelter. Effective demand is backed by ability to pay. Demand rises with household formation, migration, income and credit, and falls with high rents, house prices and borrowing costs.

Tenure is the legal arrangement under which a household occupies a home: owner-occupation, private rental, social rental, leasehold, customary or informal. Tenure affects security, maintenance and access to credit.

sections.heading: Affordability and social housing
sections.text:
Affordability is the share of income needed for rent or mortgage payments, or the house price-to-income ratio. A common rule of thumb is housing costs no more than about 30% of gross income, but definitions vary by country and lender.

Example: a household earns ₦300,000 a month, or ₦3,600,000 a year. At a 3× price-to-income ratio, an affordable purchase price is ₦10,800,000 before fees.

Social housing is subsidised or non-profit housing for low-income households, provided by government, housing associations or cooperatives. Housing policy tools include capital grants, rent subsidies, mortgage guarantees and planning rules that require affordable units.

sections.heading: Delivery and challenges
sections.text:
Delivery systems are the ways homes are built, financed and allocated. They include public construction, private developers, self-build, cooperatives and public-private partnerships, where government and private firms jointly deliver projects. Self-build means households or community groups build or extend their own homes, often in stages.

In Nigeria, delivery is constrained by expensive finance, weak title and infrastructure, high building costs and rapid urban growth; the National Housing Fund and state housing corporations are among the public tools, but many households still build incrementally. Singapore’s Housing and Development Board shows large-scale public delivery; the UK uses housing associations; South Africa has delivered large-scale subsidised housing through its Reconstruction and Development Programme.

Challenges include land assembly, servicing, construction capacity, maintenance and targeting subsidies to those in need.

keyPoints: Housing demand is want backed by ability to pay; need is the housing required for decent shelter.
Tenure is the legal arrangement of occupation, such as owner-occupation, rental, leasehold or informal.
Affordability ratio = house price ÷ annual household income; cost burden = housing cost ÷ income.
Social housing is subsidised or non-profit housing for low-income households.
Self-build means household or community construction, often in stages.
Delivery depends on land, finance, infrastructure and construction capacity; tools include subsidies, mortgages, planning and public-private partnerships.

en.title: Real Estate Agency and Marketing
en.short: Agency duties, listing, marketing, negotiation, commission and client care for property agents.

sections.heading: Agency relationship
sections.text:
An agent is authorised to act for another person, the principal. In property, the principal is usually the seller or landlord, but a buyer or tenant can also be a client. Authority may be express, such as a written agency agreement, or implied by the work. The agent owes fiduciary duties: loyalty, obedience to lawful instructions, disclosure of material facts, confidentiality and no secret profit.

The agreement should state the type of agency, such as sole agency (one agent) or multiple agency (several agents), the fee and the period. Licensing differs by country; in Nigeria, estate surveying and valuation practice is regulated by the Estate Surveyors and Valuers Registration Board of Nigeria (ESVARBON). Check the current local regulator.

sections.heading: Listing and marketing
sections.text:
Listing is the process of taking instructions and preparing property particulars: description, price or rent, size, title details and viewing arrangements. The agent should verify ownership and the client’s authority to let or sell.

Marketing chooses the target group and channels, such as online portals, signs, photographs, floor plans and inspections. Advertisements must be accurate and not misleading. Data protection and advertising rules apply, and these differ by country. Good marketing informs the market without promising a sale or rent that cannot be supported.

sections.heading: Negotiation and fees
sections.text:
Negotiation means discussing terms to reach agreement. The agent should qualify applicants, present offers promptly, record them and avoid misrepresentation. Fees may be commission, a retainer (a fixed fee for the service) or a marketing charge. Commission is often a percentage of rent or price, but rates and who pays vary by country and are negotiable.

Example only: a landlord agrees 10% commission on a first-year rent of ₦1,200,000. Commission = 0.10 × 1,200,000 = ₦120,000. If the rent is ₦1,000,000, it is ₦100,000. Client care includes clear communication, a complaints procedure, confidentiality and separate handling of client money.

keyPoints: An agent acts for a principal and owes fiduciary duties: loyalty, lawful obedience, disclosure, confidentiality and no secret profit.
The agency agreement should be written and state the agency type, fee and period.
Listing particulars and marketing must be accurate and comply with local advertising and data rules.
Agents should pass offers promptly and avoid misrepresentation during negotiation.
Commission = agreed rate × rent or price; rates, licensing and who pays differ by country, so check the agreement and local regulator.
Client money should be kept separately and complaints handled through a clear procedure.

en.title: Professional Practice and Ethics
en.short: Duties, ethics, negligence, conflicts, confidentiality, complaints and continuing development for estate surveyors.

sections.heading: Duties and bodies
sections.text: An estate surveyor and valuer gives professional advice on land and property. Professional practice means acting with competence, integrity and objectivity, in the client’s interest and the public interest. In Nigeria the professional body is the Nigerian Institution of Estate Surveyors and Valuers (NIESV), and the regulator is the Estate Surveyors and Valuers Registration Board of Nigeria (ESVARBON). ESVARBON regulates estate surveying; it is not COREN, which regulates engineering. In the United Kingdom the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) is the main professional body. Registration rules and protected titles differ by country, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: Negligence and conflicts
sections.text: Negligence is a breach of a duty of care that causes loss. A professional must meet the standard of a competent member of the profession, not perfection. The client must show duty, breach, causation and loss. A conflict of interest arises when a surveyor’s own interest, or a duty to another client, could affect advice. The safe rule is to disclose the conflict and decline or manage the instruction. A made-up case: Mrs Adeyemi asks Mr Okafor to value her shop for a bank loan. He also agrees to act for the buyer without telling either client. That is a conflict. He should disclose it and decline one side, unless both clients give informed consent in writing.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and complaints
sections.text: Confidentiality means keeping client information private. A surveyor may disclose it only with consent or where the law requires. Complaints should first go through the firm’s complaints procedure. If unresolved, they may go to the professional body or regulator, which can investigate and impose sanctions. Continuing professional development (CPD) is the ongoing learning that keeps knowledge and skills current. Many professional bodies require it, but the hours and rules vary by country and body.

keyPoints: Registration and protected titles differ by country; in Nigeria ESVARBON regulates estate surveying, not COREN.
Professional duties include competence, integrity, objectivity and regard for the public interest.
Negligence needs a duty of care, a breach, causation and loss.
Disclose conflicts of interest and decline or manage the instruction; keep client information confidential.
Complaints go first to the firm, then to the professional body or regulator.
Continuing professional development keeps skills current; requirements vary by body and country.

en.title: Advanced Valuation Theory, Risk and Uncertainty
en.short: Valuation models, behavioural bias, risk, AVMs, mass appraisal, standards and litigation.

sections.heading: Models and evidence
sections.text:
A valuation model links inputs to an estimate of value. The main families are sales comparison, income capitalisation, discounted cash flow (DCF), cost and residual. DCF discounts expected net cash flows at a risk-reflecting rate: V = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t, plus a discounted terminal value.

Market evidence limits every model. Comparables may be few, old or private, and properties are heterogeneous, so adjustments are judgemental. In thin markets, state the evidence and the assumptions openly.

sections.heading: Risk and behaviour
sections.text:
Risk is measurable: probabilities can be attached to outcomes. Uncertainty is not measurable in that way. Sensitivity analysis changes one input; scenario analysis sets consistent inputs; Monte Carlo simulation draws values from distributions. Behavioural influences include anchoring on the asking price, confirmation bias, herd behaviour and client pressure. These bias results even when the arithmetic is sound.

Example: a property may be worth 120m, 100m or 80m with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. Expected value = (0.25 × 120) + (0.5 × 100) + (0.25 × 80) = 30 + 50 + 20 = 100m. The range shows risk; the unknown future is uncertainty.

sections.heading: AVMs and standards
sections.text:
An automated valuation model (AVM) estimates value from data using statistical or machine-learning methods. Mass appraisal values many properties at one date with one model, as for property tax. Both need good data, testing and human review; they suit homogeneous property and struggle where evidence is thin.

Professional standards differ by country: the RICS Red Book (UK, used internationally), the International Valuation Standards and USPAP (United States). In Nigeria, valuers are registered by ESVARBON, the regulator, and most belong to NIESV, the professional body. Check the current edition. In litigation the valuer may act as expert witness, owing a duty to the court, not the client.

keyPoints: Valuation models: sales comparison, income capitalisation, DCF, cost and residual.
DCF: V = Σ CFt ÷ (1 + r)^t plus discounted terminal value.
Risk is measurable with probabilities; uncertainty is not.
Expected value = Σ (probability × outcome).
AVMs and mass appraisal need sound data, testing and review.
Standards differ by country: RICS Red Book, IVS, USPAP; in Nigeria, ESVARBON and NIESV.

en.title: Real Estate Investment and Portfolio Management
en.short: Portfolio theory, property returns and risk, diversification, REITs, securitisation and institutional allocation.

sections.heading: Return and risk
sections.text:
Return has income and capital growth. For one holding period, total return = (net income + end value − start value) ÷ start value. Risk is the chance that realised return differs from expectation, often measured by standard deviation (σ). Property is illiquid and valued infrequently, so reported volatility may understate risk.

Example: a property bought for 10,000,000 earns net income 800,000 and is sold for 10,500,000 after one year. Return = (800,000 + 500,000) ÷ 10,000,000 = 13%.

sections.heading: Portfolio theory
sections.text:
