Portfolio theory combines assets to balance expected return against risk. Expected portfolio return is the weighted average of asset returns. Portfolio risk depends on each asset’s variance and on covariances between assets. Diversification reduces unsystematic risk, which is specific to one property or firm, but not systematic risk, which affects the whole market. Asset allocation is the split across property, equities, bonds and cash.

Example: equal weights in assets with expected returns 8% and 12% give 0.5 × 8% + 0.5 × 12% = 10%.

sections.heading: REITs and securitisation
sections.text: A real estate investment trust (REIT) is a company or trust that owns income-producing property and distributes most of its income to shareholders; many are listed on a stock exchange, and rules differ by country, for example in the United States, the United Kingdom, South Africa and Nigeria. REITs give small investors liquid exposure to property. Securitisation pools loans, such as mortgages, and sells claims on their cash flows as securities. Residential mortgage-backed securities and commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) transfer loan risk to investors. The 2007 to 2009 financial crisis showed that complex securitisation can spread losses.

sections.heading: Institutional allocation
sections.text: Pension funds, insurers and endowments hold property for income, inflation hedging and diversification. They use direct holdings, pooled funds, REITs and debt. In the United States, endowments and pension funds use REITs and CMBS; in the United Kingdom, pension schemes use pooled property funds; in Nigeria, pension funds may use approved property vehicles under PenCom rules, but limits change, so check the current regulation.

keyPoints: Total return is (net income + end value − start value) ÷ start value.
Expected portfolio return is Σ (weight × expected return) for each asset.
Risk is often measured by standard deviation; Sharpe ratio = (return − risk-free rate) ÷ standard deviation.
Asset allocation is the split across property, equities, bonds and cash; diversification lowers unsystematic risk but not systematic risk.
A REIT is a property company or trust that distributes most of its income; securitisation pools loans into tradable securities.
Institutional property allocation depends on liabilities, liquidity, horizon and governance, and rules differ by country.

en.title: Sustainable Real Estate and Climate Risk
en.short: Green buildings, energy performance, ESG, lifecycle carbon, resilience and climate risk in property.

sections.heading: Green buildings and energy
sections.text: A green building is designed, built and operated to cut environmental harm, mainly energy, water and waste. Energy performance is how much energy a building uses for heating, cooling, lighting and hot water, often measured as kWh/m² per year or shown as an energy rating. A building can be certified and still use more energy than predicted; this is the performance gap. Certification schemes are voluntary and differ by country: BREEAM in the UK, LEED in the US and internationally, EDGE from IFC, Green Star in Australia. Building codes and energy rules are national or local, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: ESG and lifecycle carbon
sections.text: ESG means environmental, social and governance criteria used by investors. Environmental covers carbon, energy and waste; social covers health, safety and community; governance covers management and disclosure. Lifecycle carbon, or whole life carbon, adds embodied carbon (materials and construction) to operational carbon (energy in use) and end-of-life emissions. Measuring it needs data and assumptions, so compare like with like.

sections.heading: Climate risk and resilience
sections.text: Climate risk has two parts. Physical risk is damage from floods, heat, storms and drought. Transition risk is loss from policy, technology or market shifts, such as carbon pricing or changing demand. Resilience is the ability to withstand and recover. Measures include flood defence, shading, passive cooling, backup power and insurance. Adaptation reduces physical risk; mitigation reduces emissions.

sections.heading: Value, cost and investment
sections.text: Sustainability affects value through income, cost and risk. Lower energy bills and better comfort can raise rent and demand, sometimes called a green premium; poor performance can cause a brown discount. Upfront green costs may be higher, but operating costs fall. Regulation and disclosure can make poor buildings harder to sell or finance. Evidence varies by market, so do not assume a premium. Example: a made-up Lagos office retrofit costs ₦12,000,000 and saves ₦2,400,000 a year. Simple payback = 12,000,000 ÷ 2,400,000 = 5 years. At an illustrative 8% yield, the saving alone supports 2,400,000 ÷ 0.08 = ₦30,000,000 of value.

keyPoints: Green buildings cut energy, water and waste, but certification does not guarantee actual performance.
Energy performance is often measured in kWh/m² per year or by a national rating; rules differ by country.
ESG covers environmental, social and governance factors used in investment decisions.
Lifecycle carbon = embodied + operational + end-of-life carbon.
Climate risk includes physical risk and transition risk; resilience is the capacity to withstand and recover.
Simple payback = cost ÷ annual saving; sustainability affects value through income, cost and risk, but evidence varies by market.

en.title: Research Methods and Dissertation
en.short: Research design, literature review, methods, property data, sampling, analysis, ethics and dissertation writing.

sections.heading: Design and literature
sections.text:
Research design is the plan that links your question to evidence. It states the question, the data needed and how you will analyse them.

The literature review surveys existing work, identifies gaps and shapes the question; it is not a list of summaries. Use primary sources and cite them properly. A conceptual framework shows the ideas you will test or explore.

sections.heading: Methods and data
sections.text:
Qualitative methods explore meanings through interviews, observation and documents. Quantitative methods measure variables with surveys or secondary data. Mixed methods combine both.

Property data sources include land registries, valuation rolls, planning records, national statistical offices and commercial databases. These sources change over time, so check the current official source and record the date you accessed it.

sections.heading: Sampling and analysis
sections.text:
Sampling selects cases from a population. Probability sampling, such as simple random or stratified sampling, supports statistical inference. Non-probability sampling, such as purposive or convenience sampling, is common in qualitative work but limits generalisation.

Example: a population of 500 properties has 300 residential and 200 commercial. A sample of 50 allocated proportionally gives 30 residential and 20 commercial. Analysis must match the method: descriptive and inferential statistics for quantitative data; thematic analysis for qualitative data.

sections.heading: Ethics, writing, limits
sections.text:
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality, avoidance of harm and honesty in data. Dissertation writing follows a clear structure: introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion and conclusion. Use consistent referencing.

State limitations plainly: they explain what the design cannot show and how this affects your conclusions. Limitations are not failures; they set the boundaries of your claims. Keep a data access log. Acknowledge data gaps and changing official figures.

keyPoints: Research design links the research question to the evidence and the analysis.
A literature review identifies gaps in existing knowledge; it is not a list of summaries.
Qualitative methods explore meaning, while quantitative methods measure variables.
Property data sources change over time, so check the current official source and record the access date.
For proportional stratified sampling, nh = (Nh ÷ N) × n.
Ethics require consent, confidentiality and honesty; limitations state what the design cannot show.
